Wanton
WON-ton
adjective
From Middle English wantowen: wan-, a negative prefix (“lacking, un-”), and towen, “trained, disciplined, brought up” — hence undisciplined, unbroken, untrained. The wanton is not merely lustful but ungoverned.

Biblical Definition

Wanton means undisciplined. The Middle English is wan-towen, un-trained — the word for a colt never broken to the bridle — and every biblical use turns on that root. Isaiah names it in the eye: the daughters of Zion “are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet” (Isa 3:16). The Hebrew is the eye that ogles, that goes wandering after what it wants; the neck is stretched, the step is studied, the very ankles are made to ring — a whole body trained to be looked at and untrained to any other law. Paul uses the word of the heart’s revolt: the younger widows, he says, “when they have begun to wax wanton against Christ, they will marry” (1Ti 5:11). Wanton against Christ — the Greek pictures the young beast kicking against the rein it once bore. Desire that will not be governed does not merely wander; it turns and strikes at the hand that holds it. And James lays the word on the rich oppressors in the day of judgment: “Ye have lived in pleasure on the earth, and been wanton; ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter” (Jas 5:5). Fattening the heart on pleasure while the sentence is being pronounced — that is wantonness at its ripest. Ezekiel sums the end of it in two words: “the lewd women” (Eze 23:44). Wantonness begins as a look and ends as an identity.

Webster 1828 Definition

Undisciplined, unrestrained, ungoverned; hence lascivious, loose, and given to unbridled desire.

WANTON, wandering or roving in gaiety; licentious; lascivious; unrestrained; not governed by law or moral restraint.

From Middle English wan-towen: wan-, un-, and towen, “trained, disciplined.” The wanton is the unbroken colt.

Isaiah names the wanton eye among the finery of the haughty daughters of Zion (Isa 3:16).

To wax wanton against Christ is to kick against the rein once borne (1Ti 5:11).

The wanton nourish their hearts as in a day of slaughter (Jas 5:5).

Key Scripture

Isa 3:16 — "Moreover the LORD saith, Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet:"

1Ti 5:11 — "But the younger widows refuse: for when they have begun to wax wanton against Christ, they will marry;"

Jas 5:5 — "Ye have lived in pleasure on the earth, and been wanton; ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter."

Eze 23:44 — "Yet they went in unto her, as they go in unto a woman that playeth the harlot: so went they in unto Aholah and unto Aholibah, the lewd women."

Modern Corruption

Live: the age has made ungovernedness the definition of freedom, and it begins where Isaiah said it begins — in the eye.

expand to see more

Take the etymology seriously and the modern corruption stands exposed. Wanton is un-trained; and our generation has decided that to be untrained is to be free. Discipline is repression, restraint is shame, and the governed appetite is a life half-lived — so runs the creed. But Scripture says the unbroken colt is not free; it is merely useless, and eventually it is dangerous. Paul’s phrase is the one to sit with: to wax wanton against Christ. Ungoverned desire is not neutral. It does not simply wander off; it turns and kicks at the Lord who holds the rein, because a desire that will bow to nothing has already made itself a god and cannot abide a rival. The man who says he answers to no law has not escaped a master; he has only exchanged the Lord of glory for the most tyrannical master a soul can serve, which is itself.

The principle to recover is that Isaiah locates the whole disease in the eye. Before the mincing and the tinkling, before Aholah and Aholibah, there is the wanton eye — the look that goes roving after what it wants and the look that is arranged to be wanted. Both are in Isa 3:16, and both are still with us; only the ornaments have changed, and the tinkling now travels at the speed of light and into every pocket. So Job made a covenant with his eyes, and Christ said that whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart, and John warned of the lust of the eyes as one of the three things not of the Father but of the world. The cure is not a stricter watch on behaviour but a broken and bridled heart: put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means undisciplined, ungoverned — hence lascivious and unrestrained.

expand to see more

Wanton — Middle English wantowen: wan- (un-) + towen (trained).

The root picture is a colt never broken to the bridle: undisciplined, not merely lustful.

Isaiah names the wanton eye — the eye that roves and the eye arranged to be seen (Isa 3:16).

To wax wanton against Christ is to kick against the rein once borne (1Ti 5:11).

Its end is a day of slaughter with a heart fattened on pleasure (Jas 5:5).

Usage

"Wanton is un-trained: the wanton is the colt that was never broken to the bridle."

"The daughters of Zion walked with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes — a body trained to be looked at."

"To wax wanton against Christ is not to wander from the rein but to kick at the hand that holds it."
